fields.title: Cyber Threat Intelligence
fields.description: Learn how to collect, analyze, and use threat intelligence to predict attacks, prioritize risks, and make better security decisions.

fields.title: Digital Forensics
fields.description: Understand how to preserve evidence, investigate incidents, and reconstruct what happened using logs, disk artifacts, and memory analysis.

fields.title: White Hacker
fields.description: Practice ethical hacking foundations: reconnaissance, common vulnerabilities, and safe exploitation methods to improve defenses.

fields.title: AI Cyber Security
fields.description: Explore how AI is used in security: anomaly detection, phishing detection, SOC automation, and the risks of adversarial ML.

fields.title: Lecture 1
fields.heading: Threat Intelligence Basics
fields.content: Threat intelligence basics: sources, types (strategic/operational/tactical), and the intel lifecycle. Understanding how TI supports decision-making and how to integrate it into security operations.

fields.title: Lecture 2
fields.heading: IOC, IOA and ATT&CK
fields.content: IOC vs IOA, ATT&CK mapping, and how to turn raw indicators into actionable detections. Building detection rules and aligning them with adversary behavior.

fields.title: Lecture 3
fields.heading: Threat Actor Profiling
fields.content: Threat actor profiling, TTPs, reporting structure, and communicating risk to stakeholders. Writing clear TI reports and briefing non-technical audiences.

fields.title: Lecture 4
fields.heading: Collection and Automation
fields.content: Collection & automation: feeds, enrichment, scoring, and basic TI workflows for a SOC. Integrating open-source and commercial feeds into your pipeline.

fields.title: Lecture 1
fields.heading: Introduction to Digital Forensics
fields.content: Introduction to digital forensics: principles of evidence, chain of custody, and legal considerations. Role of forensics in incident response and criminal investigations.

fields.title: Lecture 2
fields.heading: Disk and File System Analysis
fields.content: Disk and file system analysis: imaging, recovery of deleted files, timeline analysis. Using common tools to extract artifacts from Windows and Linux systems.

fields.title: Lecture 3
fields.heading: Memory Forensics
fields.content: Memory forensics: capturing RAM, analyzing processes and network connections, detecting malware and rootkits. Volatility and modern memory analysis techniques.

fields.title: Lecture 4
fields.heading: Log Analysis and Reporting
fields.content: Log analysis and correlation: event logs, network logs, and building a timeline. Writing forensic reports and presenting findings in court or to management.

fields.title: Lecture 1
fields.heading: Ethics and Reconnaissance
fields.content: Ethical hacking overview: scope, authorization, and legal boundaries. Passive and active reconnaissance, OSINT, and footprinting without crossing legal lines.

fields.title: Lecture 2
fields.heading: Common Vulnerabilities
fields.content: Common vulnerabilities: OWASP Top 10, misconfigurations, and weak authentication. Identifying and documenting findings in a structured way.

fields.title: Lecture 3
fields.heading: Exploitation Basics
fields.content: Safe exploitation basics: proof-of-concept without causing damage, using labs and CTF environments. Understanding exploit development and mitigation.

fields.title: Lecture 4
fields.heading: Reporting and Remediation
fields.content: Reporting and remediation: writing clear findings, risk ratings, and working with developers to fix issues. Building a sustainable offensive security program.

fields.title: Lecture 1
fields.heading: AI in Security Overview
fields.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used in cybersecurity to detect, analyze, and prevent threats. Unlike traditional security systems that operate based on predefined rules, AI-based systems can learn from data, recognize anomalies, and adapt to new attacks.

## How AI is used in cybersecurity?

1. Threat detection
AI analyzes network traffic, logs, and user behavior to identify suspicious activity, even if the attack has not been seen before (zero-day attacks).

2. Behavior analysis (Behavior Analytics)
 Machine learning systems build a "normal profile" of user or device behavior and alert if the behavior deviates from the norm (for example, logging in at an unusual time or from a different country).

3. Phishing and spam protection
AI recognizes phishing emails by analyzing the text, links, message structure, and sender behavior, making it more effective than simple filters.

4. Incident Response Automation
AI can automatically block suspicious IP addresses, disable compromised accounts, and reduce the response time to attacks.

5. Malware Analysis (Malware)
Machine learning models analyze the behavior of files and programs, rather than just their signatures, helping to detect previously unknown viruses.

## ⚠️ Limitations and risks of AI in security

False positives — AI may mistakenly block legitimate activity

Data dependence — poor or incomplete data reduces effectiveness

Attacks on AI models — attackers may try to deceive models (adversarial attacks)

Lack of transparency — it is difficult to explain why AI made a particular decision

👉 Therefore, AI complements, but does not replace, cybersecurity professionals.

fields.title: Lecture 2
fields.heading: Phishing and Malware Detection
fields.content: Phishing and malware detection with ML: feature extraction, model types, and real-world deployment. Handling false positives and keeping models up to date.

fields.title: Lecture 3
fields.heading: SOC Automation and SOAR
fields.content: SOC automation and SOAR: using AI to triage alerts, automate playbooks, and reduce analyst fatigue. Integration with SIEM and ticketing systems.

fields.title: Lecture 4
fields.heading: Adversarial ML and Risks
fields.content: Adversarial ML and AI risks: evasion, poisoning, and model theft. Defending ML systems and understanding the limits of AI in security.
